items.name: text
items.title: Text
items.description: Paragraph text and the wrappers that pick the element for you: H1-H4, Span, and Label. Size, tone, weight and align are props; tone names a role (default, quiet, primary, danger, on-primary, on-danger) rather than a colour, so it follows the palette and mode. Heading level and size are independent, so the semantically correct level never forces a look. No loading state - place a Skeleton yourself, at the height the real text will take.

items.name: stack
items.title: Stack
items.description: VStack stacks children downward and HStack lays them out sideways, both with an 8px gap you never have to ask for. Gap takes Tailwind's own spacing scale rather than a second scale; align and justify are ordinary props, and HStack centres across the row because a row is nearly always something small beside a line of text. No loading state and no empty state - a stack takes arbitrary children, so it cannot tell empty from one child that renders nothing; place a Skeleton yourself. asChild makes the single child the stack rather than wrapping it in a div, which is how List gets its <ul> without a second gap scale.

items.name: page
items.title: Page
items.description: The background everything else sits on: it sets the page colour, the text colour and a full-viewport min height, and nothing else in the kit does. Without it a card floats on browser-default white and quiet text is unreadable in dark mode. It adds no padding and no max width, because a page is not always a column of prose. Page is a div, so the real <body> behind it stays white - visible on a rubber-band scroll and behind any short page. Paint the body too: <html suppressHydrationWarning> and <body className="bg-page text-text">. The suppressHydrationWarning is not optional either - the theme script sets attributes on <html> before React starts, and React reports that as a mismatch.

items.name: surface
items.title: Surface
items.description: A box with no meaning: the card colour, a corner radius and padding, in three forms. Plain is the default and has neither border nor shadow; OutlineSurface draws a hairline edge in the border role; RaisedSurface lifts off the page with a small shadow. The forms are defined once here, so every other box in the kit - Card, ListItem - inherits them and nothing drifts. There is no PlainSurface, because Surface already is it. The shadow colour is keyed to the mode rather than to how light the page is, so raised also separates by its card colour and the shadow is a second signal, not the only one. Padding and radius are ordinary defaults - override them from outside with className when a surface holds an image to its own edges. asChild makes the single child the box rather than wrapping it in a div, which is what Card and ListItem are built on - a card that is entirely a link has to be an <a>, not a div with an <a> round it.

items.name: skeleton
items.title: Skeleton
items.description: A placeholder for content that has not arrived yet. The caller knows the height the real content will take, so they pick the size - it defaults to a single 16px bar, full width, which is right for a line of body copy. Lines stacks that many bars with a gap, last one shorter to read as text; width and height take any CSS length ("200px", "50%", 200 as px). Animation holds still for readers who asked for reduced motion, through a CSS media query rather than a JS hook, so the component stays server-renderable.

items.name: separator
items.title: Separator
items.description: A real dividing line, not a border on a neighbour. Horizontal by default (a hairline across, h-px w-full) and vertical when asked (w-px h-full). Carries role="separator" and data-orientation so it is visible in the accessibility tree and styleable from outside. Paints the border role and is shrink-proof inside a flex row, so it does not collapse when neighbours grow.

items.name: empty-state
items.title: EmptyState
items.description: What to show when there is nothing to show. A centred stack with an optional icon, a title, a quiet description and a place for an action (usually a button). It adds no background and no card of its own - the caller decides where it sits and how tall its container is. Inside a List the empty slot renders it; on its own it centres within whatever box it is given. Title is a heading, description is quiet text, icon is muted and centred.

items.name: button
items.title: Button
items.description: A real <button> in four paints - PrimaryButton fills with the primary colour, GhostButton has no fill until you point at it, LinkButton looks like a link but is still a button, DangerButton is for anything you would want a moment to reconsider. variant="default" is accepted as a silent alias for primary, because that is the word shadcn habit types. Size is an ordinary prop: sm, md, lg at 32, 40 and 48px, all clear of the 24px minimum target size. The height is a minimum rather than a fixed height, so a long label grows the button instead of spilling out of it. The focus ring is a 2px outline in the focus-ring role, offset by 2px, on :focus-visible and never on :focus - :focus would put a ring on every mouse click. It is server-renderable as written; attaching an onClick makes the caller's file browser-only, not this one.

items.name: card
items.title: Card
items.description: A standalone box with content parts: CardMedia, CardTitle, CardBody, CardFooter. It is a Surface with the raised form as its default, laid out as a column with a gap. CardTitle renders no heading of its own - put an H2 or H3 inside it, at the level the surrounding page actually needs, because a level hardcoded here would be wrong about half the time. Surface owns the card's padding, so CardMedia reaches the edges by cancelling it, taking the top when it is first, the bottom when it is last, and both when it is the only part. CardBody takes the leftover height, so footers line up across a row of cards with different titles. The card is what sets position: relative, so a CardLink inside can stretch to cover it. asChild makes the card the element it stands in for - use it only when nothing inside the card is clickable too; when anything is, reach for CardLink. For a row inside a list, use ListItem instead: a list row is only valid inside a list. CardMedia's cancel margin is the exact negative of Surface's padding and knows that number rather than reading it, so if you override the card's padding the two have to move together - p-6 on the card wants -mx-6 on the media.

items.name: card-link
items.title: CardLink
items.description: Makes the whole Card around it clickable without wrapping the card in an anchor. The obvious move - Card asChild round an <a> - is wrong the moment the card contains anything else clickable, because interactive elements cannot nest, and every post card has tags, so that is the normal case rather than the edge case. Card sets position: relative and the link grows a pseudo-element that covers it: the card is clickable everywhere, the tags inside still take their own clicks, and there is one link in the accessibility tree rather than one per element. The focus ring goes on the overlay, so tabbing to a card outlines the card. Two accepted costs: text inside a stretched-link card cannot be selected, and anything else interactive has to sit above the overlay - CardFooter already does, so put clickable things there or give yours position: relative. asChild lets a framework's own Link component be the link. Put it in the title, not the footer: the overlay covers the nearest positioned ancestor, and CardFooter is positioned, so a CardLink inside a footer stretches over the footer alone and the rest of the card silently stops being clickable.

items.name: list-item
items.title: ListItem
items.description: One row inside a List. It renders an <li>, so it is only valid inside a list - a box that stands on its own is a Card instead, with the same parts and a different wrapper. It is a Surface in the plain form by default, because rows sit against each other and a list of outlined boxes reads as a stack of unrelated things. CardListItem is the named wrapper for the raised form - a row that looks like a card - not a second component. The row is positioned, so a CardLink inside it works exactly as it does inside a Card and the focus ring lands on the whole row. List supplies the <ul> and the gap between rows; asChild replaces the row element, and whatever you pass should still be an <li>.

items.name: list
items.title: List
items.description: A proper list that owns the gap between rows, the empty state and the loading state - which the stacks deliberately do not, because a stack takes arbitrary children and cannot tell an empty list from one child that renders nothing. renderItem returns the contents of a row, not the row element: List wraps each one in a ListItem, so every row is a real <li>. It never truncates - the old kit's list silently rendered the first three items and dropped the rest - and it keeps the header in every state, where the old one returned early while loading and took the header with it. Precedence is error, then loading, then empty, and empty only when items is actually empty. Loading renders placeholder rows so the block keeps a list-shaped height instead of collapsing. gap takes Tailwind's spacing scale; getKey falls back to the index, which is wrong the moment the list is reordered.

items.name: badge
items.title: Badge
items.description: A pill that is a real <button> - the tag on a card and the toggle in a filter bar are the same component, because a tag you can click and a tag you cannot should not look like two different things. There is no variant at all: unselected and selected are states, and a filled variant would be a second way to say selected. Unselected is outlined with the input border, which is the role built to clear 3:1, since the outline is the only thing marking the control. Selected fills with the primary colour rather than the highlight - no pale tint reaches 3:1, and a selected tag is reporting the state of a control - and it also changes text colour and weight, so the two states do not differ by hue alone. aria-pressed carries the state to a screen reader. The badge never holds the state itself: onSelectedChange asks for the opposite of what it currently is, and the caller decides. A caller's own onClick runs first and can preventDefault to stop the toggle. Heights match Button's 32 / 40 / 48px, all well clear of the 24px minimum target size, which matters most here because a tag toggle is the smallest clickable thing in the kit.

items.name: search-field
items.title: Search Field
items.description: A real <input type="search"> with the magnifier and the clear button a reader expects to find on one. Unlike Button and Badge, this one is marked browser-only: those become browser-only in the caller's file when a handler is attached there, whereas a search field has nowhere to be but the browser, because onValueChange is the whole point of it. It never holds the text - value and onValueChange belong to the caller, which is what lets FilterBar keep the input immediate while it delays the filtering behind it. The clear button is a state rather than a prop and has no way to switch it off: it appears when there is something to clear, and it is a real button so it can be tabbed to, which the browser's own is not in every engine. WebKit's native clear button is suppressed so there are not two; Firefox draws none at all, which is the reason ours exists. The field has no visible label, so the placeholder becomes its accessible name unless the caller passes one. The background is transparent and only the input border is drawn, so the same field sits correctly on the page and inside a card without being told which. Heights match Button and Badge at 32 / 40 / 48px, and the horizontal padding is the height on both sides - room for the magnifier at the start and for the clear button, which is exactly that square. Insets use logical properties, so both swap ends in a right-to-left language instead of crossing the text. className lands on the wrapper, which is the box a caller sizes; everything else spreads onto the input.

items.name: filtering
items.title: Filtering
items.description: The one piece of real logic in the kit, and it ships as plain functions - no React, no dependencies - so a route handler, a build script or a test can use it as readily as a component. It knows nothing about posts or any other shape: you tell it how to read tags and text out of your own objects through an accessors argument. filterItems keeps what matches the text and the tags, preserving input order, and hands back the very same array when nothing is selected, so a useMemo above it has an unchanged reference to compare. Several tags narrow by default - an item must carry all of them - and match: 'any' flips that to widening. Text search ignores case and accents in three steps: decompose, drop the Latin combining marks, then recompose; that last step is not optional, because decomposing splits a Korean syllable into its parts and skipping the recompose would compare split text against unsplit and match nothing, breaking the exact languages the accent-stripping was meant to leave alone. Search matches anywhere in the text, not only at word starts, and combines with tags using and. collectTags counts every item whatever is selected, for a static tag cloud; collectTagsWithSelection recounts against the criteria in force and marks each tag selected or disabled, for a live filter bar - a tag that would leave the reader with nothing greys out, and a tag that is already on is never disabled, because the question asked is whether adding it would empty the list, not whether toggling it would. Both order tags by count, highest first, then alphabetically on a tie, because that order is visible on screen and wrong is not something anyone can spot by eye. Tag matching is exact and case-sensitive, and a tag twice on one item counts once. toggleTag always returns a new array.

items.name: use-filtered-items
items.title: useFilteredItems
items.description: filterItems, memoized, with the typing caught up to. Only the text is delayed, by 200ms: the caller's own input value is never touched, so the field stays immediate - a delayed input feels broken rather than fast. Tags are not delayed either, because a click is one event rather than a stream and waiting after one looks like a dropped press. It returns the items together with the criteria they were actually filtered by, and that second half is not a convenience: anything else on screen that has to agree with the results - a tag row greying out the tags that lead nowhere - must be computed from the same delayed criteria, or it runs a whole keystroke ahead of the list and greys out tags while the results contradicting them are still on screen. The memo depends on the two accessor functions rather than the object holding them, and on a key derived from the selected tags rather than the array itself, since both are written inline at nearly every call site and would otherwise be new on every render; hoist the accessors to a module constant or a useCallback or the memo has nothing to hold on to. It ships with useDelayedValue, the general hook underneath it: the value arriving late, starting at whatever it was given so a first render never waits, and thereafter waiting for the value to hold still.

items.name: filter-bar
items.title: Filter Bar
items.description: A search field and a row of tag toggles - where SearchField, Badge and the filtering functions meet. It holds nothing: query and selected belong to the caller, because those same two values are what useFilteredItems needs, and a bar keeping its own copy would leave the caller reading the filter state back out of the UI. tags takes plain strings, or the objects collectTagsWithSelection returns; pass those and a tag that would leave the reader with nothing greys out before it is pressed. There is nothing to configure - the shape handed in is the behaviour that comes out. A selected tag is never disabled however it arrives, because greying out the tag under the finger that just pressed it reads as a bug and traps the reader in a filter they cannot lift. onSelectedChange is handed the whole new selection rather than the tag that moved, so callers store what they are given instead of reimplementing toggleTag at every call site. The tag row is a named group, so a screen reader arriving at the first pressed button is told what the row is for, and it wraps rather than scrolling sideways, because a tag pushed off the end of a scroller is a filter nobody learns exists.

items.name: post-layouts
items.title: Post Layouts
items.description: Two post layouts - one card-shaped, one row-shaped - shipped as examples to copy rather than components to configure. A post has a cover, a title, a date, tags and an excerpt, and that shape belongs to your site rather than to a UI kit, so the arrangement is given as source to edit. There are two on purpose: the same five fields out of the same pieces, which is what proves the pieces recombine. PostCard stands on its own and is clickable everywhere, with the CardLink in the title rather than the footer, because the overlay covers the nearest positioned ancestor and CardFooter is positioned - put the link there and only the footer stays clickable. PostRow renders the contents of a row rather than the row itself, so it goes straight into a List's renderItem, and its thumbnail is fixed width and never shrinks, or a long title collapses it to a sliver. The tags in both sit above the stretched link, or it swallows their presses. The date is a real time element with the machine-readable value in the attribute, formatted with the locale and the time zone both named, because a server and a browser in different zones format the same instant differently and React calls that a hydration mismatch. Covers carry an empty alt, since the title beside them already says what they are. An example becomes a real component when the same shape has held up across three separate uses without changing - not before.
